title: Angry Young Indians Flood Streets, Rally Against Modi’s Policies in Nationwide Protests
body:
A wave of youthful dissent surged through the streets of New Delhi on Saturday, as thousands of students, recent graduates and first‑time voters gathered to protest a controversial clean‑up of India’s electoral rolls. Demonstrators argue that the removal of millions of names—officially presented as a fight against duplicate and bogus entries—disproportionately targets supporters of opposition parties and threatens the democratic participation of a generation that had hoped the 2024 general election would be a turning point. Police responded with a heavy‑handed crackdown, deploying tear gas, water cannons and mass arrests, yet many participants, including 22‑year‑old economics student Kashish Rawat, vowed to keep the fight alive.

Rawat’s story epitomizes the resolve behind the protests. Without informing her parents, she traveled from her hometown in Uttar Pradesh to the capital, intent on joining a rally organized by a coalition of student unions and civil‑society groups. Upon arrival, she was met with a cordoned‑off police perimeter and a barrage of loudspeakers warning of “illegal assembly.” Undeterred, Rawat slipped through a side gate, joined a crowd chanting “Vote for change, not for corruption,” and was later detained along with dozens of others. In a brief interview after her release, she said the purge “feels like a weapon aimed at silencing our voices,” adding that many of her peers fear being disenfranchised before they even cast their first ballot.

The electoral roll revision, announced by the Election Commission in early 2024, claims to have removed more than 1.5 million duplicate or ineligible entries nationwide. Government officials contend that the exercise is essential to safeguard the integrity of the voting process, especially after allegations of “phantom voters” in previous elections. Critics, however, point to data released by independent watchdogs that show a striking concentration of deletions in constituencies where the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) faces stiff competition. In Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh and parts of the Northeast, opposition parties have reported that up to 70 percent of the removed names belong to their supporters, raising suspicions of partisan bias.

Political analysts see the protests as a litmus test for the Modi administration’s handling of dissent ahead of the national elections slated for early 2025. “The government’s narrative of a clean election is being challenged not just by opposition leaders but by a sizable, tech‑savvy youth demographic that grew up with social media activism,” said Dr. Ananya Singh, a professor of political science at Jawaharlal Nehru University. “If the state continues to equate security with suppression, it risks alienating a voter base that could be decisive in swing states.” The BJP, meanwhile, has dismissed the demonstrations as “law‑less agitation” orchestrated by foreign‑funded NGOs, and has warned that any further disruption will be met with “strict legal action.”

Human‑rights organisations have condemned the police response as disproportionate. Amnesty International’s India desk released a statement urging authorities to respect the right to peaceful assembly and to refrain from using excessive force. The statement highlighted reports of journalists being detained and of protestors being beaten despite wearing protective gear. In response, the Ministry of Home Affairs issued a brief note claiming that “all law‑enforcement actions were within legal parameters to maintain public order” and that “any allegations of misconduct will be investigated.”

As the nation heads toward a pivotal election, the street protests underscore a broader undercurrent of frustration among young Indians who feel their future is being pre‑emptively shaped by top‑down decisions. Whether the movement can translate its street energy into electoral impact remains uncertain, but the visibility of the dissent is undeniable. Observers expect that the Election Commission will face intensified scrutiny over its roll‑purge methodology, and that political parties will need to address the legitimacy concerns raised by the youth. In the weeks ahead, the trajectory of these demonstrations—and the government’s reaction—could well determine the tone of India’s democratic discourse as it approaches the next chapter of its electoral history.
